fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Jews ask for signs, and Greeks look for wisdom. But we proclaim Christ crucified. To Jews this is an offense they stumble over, and to Gentiles it is foolishness, but to those whom God has called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ is God’s power and God’s wisdom.

— 1 Corinthians 1:22–24

Some time in the mid-50s AD, in the city of Ephesus, Paul had two kinds of news from Corinth on his desk. One was a report brought by “Chloe’s people”, members of a household he trusted, that the church he had founded was splitting into rival camps. The other was a letter from the church itself, full of questions: about marriage, about meat from pagan temples, about spiritual gifts. Three men from Corinth, Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus, had come to see him in person.

His answer is the letter we call 1 Corinthians, though it was not the first he wrote them: he mentions an earlier one (5:9) that has not survived. It is the fullest window we have into a single early church, with all its gifts and all its mess. Paul deals with lawsuits, sex, food, dinner parties, hairstyles, chaotic worship and a collection of money, and brings every one of these ordinary matters, sooner or later, to the cross of Christ and to his resurrection.

A city and a church

Corinth stood on the narrow neck of land joining mainland Greece to the Peloponnese, with a harbour on each side: Lechaeum facing west toward Italy, Cenchreae facing east toward Asia. The Romans had destroyed the old Greek city in 146 BC, and Julius Caesar refounded it in 44 BC as a Roman colony. By Paul’s day it was the capital of the province of Achaia, rich, busy and keenly aware of status. The Isthmian Games were held nearby, which may be why Paul reaches so readily for pictures of runners and boxers.

Paul arrived around AD 50, alone and, he says, “weak and afraid”. Acts tells how he lodged with Aquila and Priscilla, Jewish believers who, like him, made tents, and how he stayed a year and a half (Acts 18:1–18). The church he left was mostly Gentile, with a few people of means and many more who had little, a mixture that lies behind much of the letter.

The shape of the letter

  • Chapters 1–4: divisions and the wisdom of the cross. The church has split into parties around favourite teachers; Paul answers with the foolishness of a crucified Messiah.
  • Chapters 5–6: the body belongs to the Lord. A case of incest the church has tolerated, believers suing one another, and visits to prostitutes.
  • Chapter 7: marriage and singleness. Paul begins answering their letter.
  • Chapters 8–10: food offered to idols. Knowledge, love, freedom and the conscience of others, with Paul’s own life as the example.
  • Chapters 11–14: when the church gathers. Head coverings, the Lord’s Supper, spiritual gifts, the body of Christ, love, tongues and prophecy.
  • Chapter 15: the resurrection of the dead.
  • Chapter 16: the collection, travel plans and greetings.

The repeated “Now about” (7:1, 7:25, 8:1, 12:1, 16:1, 16:12) probably marks each new question from the Corinthians’ letter.

Christ crucified

The trouble Paul tackles first is the one he cares about most. “I am for Paul,” “I am for Apollos,” “I am for Cephas,” “I am for Christ.” The church had turned its teachers into banners. His response is a set of short, stinging questions: “Has Christ been parceled out?” “Was it Paul who was crucified for you?”

Beneath the factions Paul sees a hunger for wisdom as the world measures it, for eloquence and status. So instead of choosing a side, he goes to the cross. “To those on the way to destruction, the message of the cross is foolishness; but to us who are being saved, it is God’s power.” In that weakness God has shown his wisdom and power, and the Corinthians themselves are the proof: when God called them, “not many of you were wise as people measure wisdom, not many held power, not many came from leading families.”

Paul’s own preaching in Corinth, he reminds them, had been deliberately plain:

My decision was this: while I was among you, the only thing I would know was Jesus Christ, and him as the one who was crucified.

— 1 Corinthians 2:2

As for the teachers they rally round, they are only servants. “I planted, Apollos watered, but it was God who kept making it grow.” The church is God’s field, God’s building, and “together you are God’s temple.” Boasting in one leader over another makes no sense, because everything they have was a gift: “What do you have that was not given to you?”

The body belongs to the Lord

Chapters 5 and 6 can be uncomfortable reading. A man in the church “is living with his father’s wife”, and the church, far from grieving, is proud of its tolerance. Paul calls them to act, with the hope that the man’s spirit “may be saved” on the day of the Lord. They must clear out the old yeast, for “Christ has been sacrificed as our Passover lamb.” Believers suing one another before pagan courts would do better to accept being wronged.

Some in Corinth had a slogan: “Everything is permitted for me.” This translation, like many, puts it in quotation marks, since Paul seems to be quoting the Corinthians before he answers them: “Yes, but not everything is for the good.” Their view seems to have been that the body did not matter much; what mattered was the spirit. Paul answers that the body matters a great deal. God will raise it. It is part of Christ’s body. It is a temple of the Holy Spirit:

Or do you not know that your body is a temple where the Holy Spirit lives, the Spirit who is in you and whom God has given you? You do not belong to yourselves. You were bought, and a price was paid for you. So bring glory to God in your body.

— 1 Corinthians 6:19–20

Among the hard words of chapter 6 there is a tender one. After listing the ways of life that do not belong in God’s kingdom, Paul adds, “Some of you once lived in these ways. But you have been washed clean; you have been made holy; you have been put right with God.”

Marriage and singleness

With chapter 7 Paul turns to their letter, and the first thing in it seems to be another slogan: “It is good for a man to have no sexual contact with a woman.” Some, it appears, thought spiritual people should give up sex even within marriage. Paul disagrees. Husband and wife belong to each other, and neither should refuse the other. At the same time he values singleness, which he himself lives, as a gift that leaves a person free to give undivided care to the things of the Lord.

Paul is careful about his sources: on divorce, “it is the Lord’s, not mine”; on a believer married to an unbeliever, “it is not a word from the Lord”. Over it all lies a sense of urgency, for “this world’s present shape is passing away.”

Knowledge and love

Much of the meat sold in a city like Corinth had passed through a pagan temple, and many social occasions took place in temple dining rooms. Could a Christian eat it? The confident said yes, with a point: “no idol in the world is anything real.” Paul agrees, and then adds a sentence that sums up the whole letter:

Knowledge puffs a person up, but love builds others up.

— 1 Corinthians 8:1

The question is not only what I am free to do, but what my freedom does to “a brother or sister for whom Christ died.” In chapter 9 Paul gives himself as the example. He has every right to be paid for his preaching, and he will not use it. “To all people I have become all things, so that one way or another I may save some.” He trains like an athlete, not for “a wreath that soon withers” but for one that never decays.

Chapter 10 warns from Israel’s wilderness years, when the people drank from a rock (“that rock was Christ”) and still fell into idolatry. Then comes a promise many readers have leaned on in hard times: “God is faithful, and he will not allow the testing to go past your strength.” And a rule for all of life: “whatever you do, do everything for God’s glory.”

When you come together

Chapters 11 to 14 concern the church at worship. They open with instructions about men and women praying and prophesying with their heads covered or uncovered. This is one of the hardest passages in Paul to understand, and Christians read it in different ways: some as a lasting principle about men and women, some as guidance about the customs of a particular culture, with much discussion over whether “head” speaks of authority or of source. Paul plainly expects women to pray and prophesy aloud, and he insists, “Yet in the Lord there is no woman without man, and no man without woman.”

Then he turns to the Lord’s Supper, which in Corinth was eaten as part of a full meal. The richer members, free to arrive early, ate and drank their fill before the poorer ones came: “one is left hungry, and another is drunk.” That, says Paul, is not really the Lord’s Supper at all. And he reminds them of what he had handed on to them, in the earliest written account of the Supper we have:

What I handed on to you, I myself received from the Lord: on the night he was handed over, the Lord Jesus took bread, gave thanks and broke it, saying, “This is my body; it is for you. Do this to remember me.” He did the same with the cup once supper was over, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Every time you drink it, do this to remember me.”

— 1 Corinthians 11:23–25

Christians have understood the bread and the cup in different ways, but Paul’s practical instruction is simple: “wait for each other.”

One body, many parts

The Corinthians prized spiritual gifts, especially speaking in tongues, and some seem to have treated them as a ladder of spiritual rank. Paul begins with what all believers share: “nobody can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except through the Holy Spirit.” There are many gifts but one Spirit, and each gift “is given for the good of all.”

Then comes his most memorable picture: the church is a body, and a body needs every part. The foot cannot leave because it is not a hand. The eye cannot tell the hand, “I can do without you.” The parts that seem weakest are the most necessary. “If one part is in pain, all the parts share its pain.”

You are Christ’s body, and each of you individually is one of its parts.

— 1 Corinthians 12:27

The greatest is love

Between the gifts of chapter 12 and the order of chapter 14 Paul sets the passage on love, which is read at weddings the world over but was first written to a quarrelling church. Without love, tongues are noise, knowledge and faith are nothing, and even giving away everything does no good. Then he describes love, and every line is a portrait of what the Corinthians were not:

Love is patient; love is kind. Love does not envy, does not show off, is not puffed up. It does not behave shamefully, it does not look for its own advantage, it does not lose its temper, and it does not keep a tally of wrongs. It takes no pleasure in wrongdoing, but shares the joy of the truth. There is nothing love cannot bear, no time when it stops believing or hoping, nothing it cannot endure.

— 1 Corinthians 13:4–7

“Love never comes to an end.” The gifts belong to the present age and will be done away with. “For now we see by means of a mirror, as if in a riddle, but then we will see face to face.” Most readers take “when what is complete arrives” to mean the return of Christ; some read it as the completed New Testament, and Christians who differ over whether gifts such as tongues continue today often part ways here.

Chapter 14 applies love to worship. Prophecy, which speaks to people in words they can understand, builds up the church; tongues without interpretation build up only the speaker. “I would sooner speak five words with my mind, so as to teach others too, than thousands upon thousands of words in a tongue.” Speakers should take turns, since “God is the God of peace, not of disorder”. The chapter also contains the instruction that women keep silent in the churches (14:34–35), which Christians have read in very different ways: as a limit on a particular disruptive kind of speaking, such as questions called out during the meeting, as a wider rule for church order, or as a later note copied into the text. The chapter ends: “But let everything be done properly and in good order.”

Raised from the dead

The letter’s last great argument begins with the gospel itself, a summary Paul had received and passed on, and which most scholars think was already a fixed formula within a few years of the first Easter:

What I handed on to you, as the first and chief thing, I myself had received: that Christ died for our sins, in keeping with the Scriptures; that he was buried; that he has been raised on the third day, in keeping with the Scriptures; and that he appeared to Cephas, and after that to the Twelve.

— 1 Corinthians 15:3–5

The witnesses follow: more than five hundred at once, James, all the apostles, and “Last of all, as though to a child born before its time”, Paul himself. Some in Corinth denied any resurrection of the dead, and Paul will not let them keep a faith without it: “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is worthless, and you are still in your sins.” But Christ has been raised, “the firstfruits of those who have died”, the first sheaf of a harvest still to come.

What will that resurrection be like? Paul’s answer is a seed. “A seed you sow does not come alive unless it dies.” What rises is continuous with what was sown, and gloriously different: “It is sown in decay; it is raised imperishable.” It is a “spiritual body”, by which Paul seems to mean not a body made of spirit, but a body given life by God’s Spirit. The chapter rises to a taunt flung at death itself: “Death, where is your victory? Death, where is your sting?” And it ends not in speculation but in work: “in the Lord your hard work is never wasted.”

A real church

The last chapter returns to earth. There is a collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, to be put aside “on the first day of each week”. There are plans: Paul will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, where “a great door stands open”; Timothy may come; Apollos will not, just yet. And there is a short command that gathers up the whole letter: “Whatever you do, do it in love.”

Then Paul takes the pen from his secretary: “I, Paul, am adding this greeting with my own hand.” Among his last words is a prayer that Christians were still saying in Aramaic, the language of Jesus, in a Greek-speaking church: Marana tha, “Our Lord, come!”

1 Corinthians in the life of the church

The church in Corinth did not stop quarrelling. Around AD 96 the church in Rome wrote to it again, in the letter known as First Clement, because the Corinthians had removed their elders. “Take up the epistle of the blessed Apostle Paul,” Clement urged them, reminding them that Paul had once had to write about Cephas and Apollos and the parties formed around them. It is among the earliest references to a New Testament letter by name.

John Chrysostom preached through the letter at Antioch in forty-four homilies. Chapter 15 is read at funerals in every Christian tradition, and Handel set its words about the last trumpet in Messiah. And the words of 11:23–26 are said, in one form or another, wherever Christians break bread.

How to read 1 Corinthians

Read it as a conversation of which we hear only one side. Notice when he seems to be quoting them, and how he answers.

Notice too how often he takes a practical question back to the centre. A dispute about teachers leads to the cross. A dispute about sex leads to the body as the Spirit’s temple. A dispute about food leads to the brother or sister for whom Christ died. A dispute about gifts leads to love. And a doubt about the future leads to the risen Christ. Read it straight through at least once, to hear how chapter 13 answers chapter 1 and chapter 15 answers them all.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in 1 Corinthians are worth knowing about before you begin.

The Corinthians’ own words. Ancient Greek had no quotation marks, and scholars generally agree that Paul sometimes quotes sayings from Corinth in order to answer them. This translation marks the likeliest of these as quotations: “Everything is permitted for me” (6:12, and in a shorter form in 10:23), the saying about food and the stomach (6:13), “It is good for a man to have no sexual contact with a woman” (7:1), and “all of us have knowledge” (8:1).

“Brothers and sisters.” Paul addresses the whole church, men and women, with a word that is masculine in form. This edition prints “brothers and sisters”; the Open Word Bible lets a reader choose “brothers” instead. In the same way, those older Bibles call “saints” are here “God’s holy people”.

Love. The King James Version followed the Latin in calling the subject of chapter 13 “charity”. This translation, like most today, says “love”, and keeps the same word throughout, so that “love builds others up” in chapter 8 can be heard preparing for chapter 13.

Places where manuscripts differ. In 13:3 the manuscripts are divided between “hand over my body to the flames” and “hand over my body so that I may boast”; the earliest manuscripts have the second, but this translation follows the first. In 11:24 it reads “This is my body; it is for you”, without the words added in later copies. And 14:34–35 stands where most Bibles print it, after verse 33, though some manuscripts place those verses after verse 40.

“Christ.” The Open Word Bible lets a reader choose whether Christos reads “Christ” or “the Messiah”. This edition prints “Christ”, but it is worth remembering, when Paul preaches “Christ crucified” to Jews and Greeks, that the word means Israel’s anointed King.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 1
fields.body_html:
Greeting

From Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and from Sosthenes our brother, to the church of God in Corinth: to you who have been made holy in Christ Jesus, a holy people by God’s call, together with all who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, the Lord who is theirs as well as ours. Grace and peace to you from God our Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ.

Thanks for God’s grace in Corinth

I give thanks to my God for you at all times, because of the grace God gave you in Christ Jesus. In him you have been made rich in everything: in every kind of speaking and every kind of knowledge. In this way the witness to Christ was made firm among you, and so you fall short in no gift of grace while you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ. He will also keep you firm to the end, so that you will be free from any charge on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful. It was he who called you to share in the life of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

Rival groups in the church

Now, brothers and sisters, I urge you by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ: agree with one another, all of you, and let there be no splits among you. Let what is torn be mended, so that you are joined together, one in mind and one in purpose. I say this, my brothers and sisters, because Chloe’s people have made it clear to me that rivalries have broken out among you. What I mean is that every one of you takes a side: “I am for Paul,” “I am for Apollos,” “I am for Cephas,” “I am for Christ.” Has Christ been parceled out? Was it Paul who was crucified for you? Or were you baptized into Paul’s name? As things are, I am thankful that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one can claim you were baptized into my name. Yes, I also baptized the household of Stephanas. Beyond them, I am not aware that I baptized anyone else. For Christ did not send me to baptize; he sent me to preach the gospel, and not with polished, wise-sounding words, so that the cross of Christ would not be robbed of its force.

The cross: God’s power and God’s wisdom

To those on the way to destruction, the message of the cross is foolishness; but to us who are being saved, it is God’s power. For Scripture says, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the cleverness of the clever I will bring to nothing.” Where is the wise person? Where is the expert in the Law? Where is the skilled debater of this present age? Has God not shown the world’s wisdom to be foolishness? For in God’s wisdom the world, with all its wisdom, did not come to know him. So it was God’s good pleasure to save those who believe through the message we preach, foolishness though it seems. Jews ask for signs, and Greeks look for wisdom. But we proclaim Christ crucified. To Jews this is an offense they stumble over, and to Gentiles it is foolishness, but to those whom God has called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ is God’s power and God’s wisdom. For the foolish thing God has done is wiser than any human wisdom, and the weak thing God has done is stronger than any human strength.

Just look at your own calling, brothers and sisters. When God called you, not many of you were wise as people measure wisdom, not many held power, not many came from leading families. Instead, God chose what the world counts foolish, to put the wise to shame. God chose what the world counts weak, to put the strong to shame. God chose what the world counts low and despises, things that are nothing, to cancel out the things that are something, so that no human being could ever boast in God’s presence. It is God who has placed you in Christ Jesus, and he has become God’s wisdom for us, which means our righteousness, our holiness and our redemption. So, as Scripture says, “Whoever boasts should boast in the Lord.”

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 2
fields.body_html:
Preaching Christ crucified

For my part, brothers and sisters, when I came to you and announced God’s testimony to you, I did not come with impressive speech or superior wisdom. My decision was this: while I was among you, the only thing I would know was Jesus Christ, and him as the one who was crucified. While I was with you, I was weak and afraid, and I trembled greatly. My message and my preaching did not depend on wisdom’s power to persuade; they were proof given by the Spirit and by power, so that your faith would be grounded not in human wisdom but in the power of God.

God’s wisdom revealed by the Spirit

There is a wisdom we speak, all the same, among those who are mature. It is not the wisdom of this present age, nor of its rulers, whose power is already being brought to an end. Instead, the wisdom we speak is God’s own, a mystery that has been kept hidden. God planned it before the ages for our glory. Not one of this age’s rulers grasped this wisdom. Had they grasped it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. But this is what Scripture describes: “Things no eye ever saw and no ear ever heard, things that never rose up in any human heart: these God has made ready for those who love him.” And it is to us that God has made them known, through the Spirit. For nothing is beyond the Spirit’s searching, not even the depths of God. After all, what human being knows what is going on inside someone else? Only that person’s own spirit within knows it. In the same way, the things of God are known to no one but the Spirit of God. We, for our part, have not received the spirit of the world. We have received the Spirit who comes from God, so that we may recognize all that God has graciously given us. When we speak of these things, our words are not lessons learned from human wisdom. The Spirit teaches them, and so we explain spiritual things in words the Spirit gives.

The natural person and the spiritual person

A person who has only natural life does not welcome what belongs to the Spirit of God. It all seems foolish to such a person, who cannot grasp it, because it can be weighed rightly only by the Spirit. But the spiritual person is able to assess all things, while no one is in a position to assess such a person. For “who has ever known the mind of the Lord well enough to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 3
fields.body_html:
Still infants

As for me, brothers and sisters, I could not speak to you as people of the Spirit. I had to speak to you as people of mere flesh, as infants in Christ. Milk was what I gave you to drink, not solid food, since you could not yet take it. In fact, even now you still cannot take it, because you are still living by the flesh. For as long as there is jealousy and quarreling among you, are you not living by the flesh and behaving in a merely human way? When one of you says, “I am for Paul,” and another, “I am for Apollos,” is that not how people talk who live on a merely human level? What, then, is Apollos? And what is Paul? Servants through whom you came to believe, each doing the work the Lord assigned. I planted, Apollos watered, but it was God who kept making it grow. So the one who plants does not count for anything, nor does the one who waters. What counts is God, who gives the growth. The one who plants and the one who waters work as one, and each will be rewarded according to the labor each has done. For we are fellow workers in God’s service, and you are God’s field, God’s building.

Building on the one foundation

Using the grace God gave me, I set a foundation in place like an expert builder, and another person is now building on top of it. But each one must take care how to build on it. For there is no other foundation anyone can lay; the one already in place is Jesus Christ. If anyone builds on this foundation with gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay or straw, each builder’s work will come out into the open. The Day will make it plain, since that Day arrives in fire, and the fire itself will prove what kind of work each one has done. If what someone has built on the foundation survives, that builder will receive a reward. If someone’s work burns up, that person will suffer loss. The builder will still be saved, but only as one who comes out through the fire.

You are God’s temple

Do you not know that together you are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit lives among you? If anyone brings ruin on the temple of God, God will bring ruin on that person. The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple.

Become foolish to be wise

Let no one fool themselves. Anyone among you who thinks they are wise in this present age must become a fool in order to become wise. What this world calls wisdom is foolishness in the eyes of God, for Scripture says, “He traps the wise in their own cleverness.” And again, “The Lord knows how empty the reasonings of the wise are.” So let no one take pride in mere human beings. Everything is yours: Paul or Apollos or Cephas, the world, life or death, what is here now or what is still to come. It all belongs to you, and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 4
fields.body_html:
Managers answerable to the Lord

So people should think of us in this way: as assistants of Christ and as household managers put in charge of the mysteries of God. Now what is looked for in household managers is this: that each one proves trustworthy. For my part, it counts for very little if you put me on trial, or if any human court does. I do not even put myself on trial. I know of nothing I have done wrong, yet that is not what acquits me. The one who examines my case is the Lord. So do not pass sentence on anything ahead of time, before the Lord comes. He will shine light on what darkness now hides and bring the purposes of all hearts out into the open. Then each one will have from God whatever praise is due.

Nothing you were not given

Brothers and sisters, I have used myself and Apollos as the picture for all this, for your sake. From us you can learn what is meant by “Nothing beyond what is written,” and then none of you will be puffed up in favor of one person and against another. Who, after all, sets you above anyone else? What do you have that was not given to you? And if it was given to you, why do you take pride in it as though it were not a gift? So you are already full! You are already rich! Without us you have begun to rule as kings! If only you really did rule, so that we too could rule alongside you! As I see it, God has brought us apostles out last of all, like condemned prisoners led in to die. We have become a show for the world to watch, angels and human beings alike. We are fools because of Christ, but you are so wise in Christ! We are weak, but you are strong! You are held in honor, but we are despised. Even now, at this very hour, we are hungry and thirsty, dressed in rags, beaten, with no place to call home. We toil, working with our own hands. Insulted, we bless; persecuted, we hold out; slandered, we reply with kind words. Right up to now we are treated like the dirt the world sweeps away, the scrapings everyone throws out.

A father’s warning

I do not write this to shame you. You are my dear children, and I am giving you a father’s warning. Though you may have countless guides to bring you up in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For it was I who fathered you in Christ Jesus, through the gospel. So I urge you: take me as your example. That is the reason I have sent Timothy to you. He is my dear child in the Lord, and he can be trusted. He will bring back to your minds the way I live in Christ Jesus, the same way I teach in every church everywhere. Some have become puffed up, assuming that I will never come to see you. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills. Then I will learn, not what these puffed-up people say, but whether they have any power. For the kingdom of God shows itself in power, not in words. Which do you prefer? Am I to come to you with a rod, or with love and gentleness of spirit?

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 5
fields.body_html:
Sexual sin the church tolerates

People are actually saying that sexual immorality is going on among you, immorality of a kind that even the Gentiles do not allow: one of you is living with his father’s wife. And you are puffed up! Why were you not grieving instead, so that the man who did this would be removed from among you? As for me, I am away in body but there in spirit, and I have already reached my verdict on the man who has done such a thing, as surely as if I were with you. When you are gathered together in the name of our Lord Jesus, and my spirit is with you, together with the power of our Lord Jesus, this man is to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, with the aim that on the day of the Lord his spirit may be saved.

Clear out the old yeast

Your pride is not a good thing. Do you not realize that just a pinch of yeast makes all the dough rise? Clear out every trace of the old yeast, so that you can be a fresh batch of dough without yeast, which is what you really are. For Christ has been sacrificed as our Passover lamb. So let us keep the festival, not with old yeast, nor with yeast that is malice and wickedness, but with bread made without yeast: sincerity and truth.

Judging those inside the church

When I wrote to you in my earlier letter, I told you not to mix with sexually immoral people. I did not mean the sexually immoral people of this world in general, nor the greedy and swindlers, nor idolaters. To do that, you would need to leave the world altogether. But what I am writing to you now is this: keep away from anyone who goes by the name of brother or sister and yet is sexually immoral, greedy, an idolater, abusive, a drunkard or a swindler. Do not even sit down to eat with such a person. Is it my place to judge those outside? Are not those inside the ones you are to judge, while God judges those outside? Drive out the evildoer from among you.

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 6
fields.body_html:
Lawsuits between believers

When one of you has a dispute with another, how can you dare to take it to court before the unrighteous instead of before God’s holy people? Or do you not know that God’s holy people will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you not fit to settle the most trivial of cases? Do you not know that we will judge angels? How much more, then, the affairs of everyday life! So if you have cases about everyday matters, why do you seat as judges people who count for nothing in the church? I say this to shame you. Is there really no one among you with wisdom enough to settle a case between brothers and sisters, so that instead believers go to law against one another, and before unbelievers at that? Simply by having lawsuits against one another you are already defeated, whatever the verdict. Why not accept being wronged instead? Why not accept being cheated instead? Instead, you yourselves do the wronging and the cheating, and to your own brothers and sisters!

Those who will not inherit the kingdom

Or do you not know that people who do wrong will not receive God’s kingdom as their inheritance? Make no mistake: the sexually immoral, idolaters, adulterers, men who take the passive part in sex with men, men who go to bed with males, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, abusive people, and swindlers: none of these will receive God’s kingdom as their inheritance. Some of you once lived in these ways. But you have been washed clean; you have been made holy; you have been put right with God, in the name of the Lord Jesus and through the Spirit of our God.

Your body belongs to the Lord

“Everything is permitted for me.” Yes, but not everything is for the good. “Everything is permitted for me.” Yes, but I will not let anything become my master. “Food exists for the stomach and the stomach for food, and in the end God will do away with them both.” The body, however, does not exist for sexual immorality; it exists for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. God raised the Lord, and by his power he will raise us as well. Do you not know that your bodies are parts of Christ’s body? Am I then to take parts of Christ’s body and make them parts of a prostitute’s body? Absolutely not! Or do you not know that a man who attaches himself to a prostitute forms one body with her? For Scripture says, “The two will be united into one flesh.” But anyone who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him. Get away from sexual immorality! Whatever other sin someone commits stays outside the body, but the one who is sexually immoral sins against their very own body. Or do you not know that your body is a temple where the Holy Spirit lives, the Spirit who is in you and whom God has given you? You do not belong to yourselves. You were bought, and a price was paid for you. So bring glory to God in your body.

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 7
fields.body_html:
Marriage and sexual relations

Now about the matters you wrote of. “It is good for a man to have no sexual contact with a woman.” But because sexual immorality is all around, each man is to have relations with his own wife. Each woman, too, is to have relations with her own husband. A husband must give his wife what he owes her in marriage, and a wife must do the same for her husband. The wife does not rule over her own body; her husband does. In the same way, the husband does not rule over his own body; his wife does. Do not refuse each other, unless you both agree to it for a limited time so that you are free for prayer. Then be together again, or Satan may use your lack of self-control to tempt you. What I am saying here is a concession; it is not a command. I would like everyone to be as I am. Yet God gives each person a gift of their own, to one this way and to another that.

Now I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is a good thing for them if they stay as I am. But if they are not keeping themselves under control, let them marry, for marrying is better than burning with desire.

The Lord’s command on divorce

To those who are married I give a charge, and it is the Lord’s, not mine: a wife is not to leave her husband. If she does separate, she should either stay unmarried or be reconciled with him. And a husband is not to divorce his wife.

Married to an unbeliever

To everyone else I say this myself; it is not a word from the Lord. Suppose a brother has a wife who does not believe, and she is content to go on living with him: he must not divorce her. And if a woman has a husband who does not believe, and he is content to go on living with her, she must not divorce him. For through his wife the husband who does not believe has been made holy, and through the brother she is married to, the wife who does not believe has been made holy. If it were not so, your children would be unclean; in fact, they are holy. But if the one who does not believe chooses to separate, let the separation happen. A brother or a sister is not bound in circumstances like these. It is in peace that God has called us. How can you tell, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how can you tell, husband, whether you will save your wife? Whatever the case, each of you should lead the life the Lord has given you, the life you had when God called you. I give this same direction in every church. Was someone already circumcised when he was called? He must not try to reverse it. Was someone uncircumcised when he was called? He must not get circumcised. Being circumcised means nothing, and not being circumcised means nothing. What matters is obeying the commandments of God. Each of you should go on in the place in life where God’s call found you.

Called as a slave or as free

Were you a slave when you were called? Do not let that worry you. But if you do get the chance to become free, make the most of it. For a slave who has been called in the Lord is the Lord’s freed slave; and in the same way, someone free who has been called is a slave of Christ. You were bought, and a price was paid for you. Do not become slaves of human beings. So, brothers and sisters, whatever your situation was when God called you, remain in it, living in God’s presence.

Those who have never married

Now about those who have never married: I have no command from the Lord, but I give my opinion as someone the Lord in his mercy has made trustworthy. So, because of the crisis we now face, I think this is good: it is good for a person to stay as they are. Are you bound to a wife? Do not try to get free. Are you free of a wife? Do not look for a wife. Yet if you do marry, you have done nothing sinful. And if a young woman who has never married takes a husband, she has done nothing sinful. But such people will meet hardship in this earthly life, and I am trying to spare you. Here is my point, brothers and sisters: the time has been cut short. So from now on, married men should be as though they had no wives, those who weep as though they did not weep, those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice, those who buy as though they kept nothing, and those who deal with the world as though they did not use it to the full. For this world’s present shape is passing away.

Undivided devotion to the Lord

I want you to be free from cares that divide you. The unmarried man gives his care to the things of the Lord, how he may please him. But the married man gives his care to the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is pulled two ways. And the unmarried woman, or the young woman who has never married, gives her care to the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body as well as in spirit. But the married woman gives her care to the things of the world, how she may please her husband. I tell you this to help you, not to throw a noose over you. I want you to live as is fitting and to stay close beside the Lord with nothing to draw you away.

Now if a man thinks he is not treating the woman he is engaged to rightly, because his desire for her is strong and the marriage ought to go ahead, he may do what he wants. He commits no sin. Let the two of them marry. But suppose a man stands firm in his heart. He is under no pressure, he has control over his own will, and he has decided in his own heart that the woman he is engaged to should stay as she is. He will do well. So the man who marries the woman he is engaged to does well, and the man who does not marry her will do better.

Widows

A wife remains bound for as long as her husband is living. Should her husband die, she is free to marry whomever she wants, though only a man who belongs to the Lord. Even so, in my opinion she is more blessed if she remains a widow. And I believe that I too have the Spirit of God.

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 8
fields.body_html:
Food offered to idols

Now about food offered to idols. We know, as you say, that “all of us have knowledge.” Knowledge puffs a person up, but love builds others up. If anyone imagines they have mastered some piece of knowledge, they have not yet come to know in the way one must. But if someone loves God, that person is known by him.

One God, one Lord

So, to come back to eating food offered to idols: we know that “no idol in the world is anything real,” and that “there is no God except one.” There may indeed be beings called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, and in that sense there are many gods and many lords. Yet for us there is one God, the Father. Everything has its source in him, and our life is directed to him. And there is one Lord, Jesus Christ. Everything exists through him, and through him we exist.

Do not make the weak fall

But not all have this knowledge. Some, from long habit with the idol up to the present, still eat the food as something offered to an idol; and their conscience, which is weak, is soiled. Food will not decide how we stand before God: we gain nothing by eating, and we lose nothing by not eating. But be careful that this right you have does not trip up those who are weak. For suppose someone who is weak sees you, the one with knowledge, reclining at a meal in an idol’s temple. Will that not “build up” their conscience, so that they go on to eat food offered to idols? And so, through your knowledge, the one who is weak is ruined: a brother or sister for whom Christ died. When you sin like this against your brothers and sisters and deal a blow to their weak conscience, you are sinning against Christ. That is why, if food causes my brother or sister to fall, I will not eat meat as long as I live, so that I will not be what makes my brother or sister fall.

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 9
fields.body_html:
The rights of an apostle

Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you not what my work in the Lord has produced? Others may not count me as an apostle, but to you I certainly am one. For you yourselves, in the Lord, are the seal that proves my apostleship.

This is my defense to those who put me on trial: Surely we have the right to be given food and drink? Surely we have the right to take a believing wife with us on our travels, as the other apostles do, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas? Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to stop working for a living? Who ever serves in an army and pays his own costs? Who plants a vineyard and eats none of its grapes? Who tends a flock and gets none of its milk? Am I saying this only on human authority? Does the law not say the same thing? For in the law of Moses it is written, “Do not muzzle an ox that is threshing grain.” Is it oxen that God is concerned about here? Or is he not surely speaking for our sake? Yes, this was written with us in mind: the one who plows ought to do so in hope, and the one who threshes ought to work expecting a share of the harvest. We sowed among you the things of the Spirit. Is it so much to ask, then, that we reap from you the things the body needs? If others share in this right to your support, do we not have a greater claim to it? Yet we never claimed this right. We put up with every hardship so as not to block the path of the gospel of Christ in any way. Do you not know that those who carry out the temple’s sacred work get their food from the temple, and those who wait on the altar receive a portion of what is offered on it? In just this way the Lord directed that those who announce the gospel should live from the gospel.

But I have not made use of any of these rights. I have not written this to have it done for me. I would rather die than that. No one will take away my reason to be proud! Preaching the gospel gives me no reason to be proud, for I am under compulsion. It will go hard with me if I do not preach the gospel! If I did this by my own choice, I would have a reward. But if it is not my choice, I have simply been entrusted with a household manager’s task. What, then, is my reward? It is this: when I preach the gospel, I offer it at no cost to anyone, and so I do not use to the full the right I have in the gospel.

All things to all people

No one has any claim on me, yet I have become everyone’s slave, so as to win over a greater number. And so to the Jews I became as a Jew, to win Jews over. For the sake of those under the law I became as one under the law, though I am not myself under the law, to win over those under the law. To those without the law I became as one without the law, to win over those without the law. Yet I am not without God’s law; I live within the law of Christ. With the weak I became weak, to win over the weak. To all people I have become all things, so that one way or another I may save some. Everything I do is for the gospel’s sake, so that I may have my share in it together with them.

Running to win the prize

Do you not know that every runner in the stadium races, yet only one is given the prize? Run like that one, so as to win it. Every competitor holds back from many things in training. They accept this to win a wreath that soon withers; we, to win one that never decays. That is how I run: not like a runner unsure of the finish. That is how I box: not like a fighter swinging at empty air. Rather, I punish my body with blows and treat it as my servant, so that after preaching to others I will not myself be found disqualified.

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 10
fields.body_html:
Warnings from Israel’s history

For I want you to grasp this, brothers and sisters: every one of our ancestors was under the cloud, and every one of them went through the sea. All of them were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. All of them ate the same spiritual food, and all of them drank the same spiritual drink. They drank from a spiritual rock that went along with them, and that rock was Christ. Yet God took no pleasure in most of them, for the wilderness was strewn with their bodies.

These events became examples for us, warning us not to crave what is evil, as they craved it. Do not become idolaters, as some of them did. Scripture says, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and then rose to make merry.” Nor should we give ourselves to sexual immorality, which some of them practiced, and 23,000 fell dead in a single day. Nor should we try the patience of Christ, as some of them tried it; they were killed off by the snakes, one after another. Do not grumble against God, the way some of them grumbled, only to perish at the hand of the Destroyer. What happened to them was meant as an example, and it was written down to warn us, who live at the time when the ages reach their end. So anyone who feels sure of standing should watch out, or they may fall. The testing that has gripped you is only what all people face. But God is faithful, and he will not allow the testing to go past your strength. Along with the testing he will also make the way out, so that you are able to hold up under it.

The Lord’s table and the table of demons

So then, my dear friends, run from idolatry. I am talking to you as people with good sense. Weigh for yourselves what I am saying. When we bless the cup of blessing, are we not given a share in the blood of Christ? When we break the bread, are we not given a share in the body of Christ? There is one loaf, and so we, though many, are one body, because we all share in that one loaf. Look at Israel, the nation by human descent. Do not the people who eat from the sacrifices share in the altar? What am I saying, then? That food offered to idols amounts to anything? Or that an idol is anything at all? No. I mean that what people sacrifice to idols, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. And I do not want you to become partners with demons. It is impossible for you to drink from the Lord’s cup and from a cup of demons as well, or to eat at the Lord’s table and at a demons’ table. Or do we mean to stir up the Lord’s jealousy? Do we think we are stronger than he is? “Everything is permitted.” Yes, but not everything is for the good. “Everything is permitted.” Yes, but not everything builds others up. No one should look for their own advantage, but for the other person’s. You may eat whatever is on sale in the meat market without asking questions for conscience’ sake, because “the earth belongs to the Lord, and everything that fills it.” Suppose an unbeliever asks you to dinner and you decide to go. Then eat whatever is served, and do not ask questions for conscience’ sake. But if anyone points out to you, “This came from a temple sacrifice,” leave it uneaten. Do so out of regard for the person who pointed it out, and because of conscience. By conscience I mean the other person’s, not yours. For why should another person’s conscience pass judgment on my freedom? If I eat my share with gratitude, why should anyone speak evil of me over food for which I thank God? So then, when you eat, when you drink, whatever you do, do everything for God’s glory. Do not trip anyone up, not Jews, not Greeks, not the church of God. I do the same: in all I do I seek to please all people, looking not for what helps me but for what helps the many, so that they may be saved.

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 11
fields.body_html:
Take me as your model, just as I take Christ as mine.

Covering the head in worship

I praise you, because you keep me in mind in everything, and you hold firmly to the traditions in the form I passed them on to you. But there is something I want you to understand: Christ is the head of every man, man is the head of woman, and God is the head of Christ. Any man who prays or prophesies with something covering his head brings shame on his head. But a woman who prays or prophesies with nothing over her head shames her head; it is no different from having her head shaved. If a woman does not wear a covering, let her have her hair cropped too. But if having her hair cropped or shaved off is shameful for a woman, then she should wear a covering. A man should not have his head covered, because he is God’s image and glory. Woman, for her part, is man’s glory. Man was not made from woman; woman was made from man. Nor was man created for the sake of woman; woman was created for the sake of man. For this reason, and because of the angels, a woman should have authority over her head. Yet in the Lord there is no woman without man, and no man without woman. Just as woman was made from man, so man is born through woman, and all things have their source in God. Use your own judgment. When a woman prays to God, is it fitting for her head to be uncovered? Is it not nature itself that teaches you this: for a man, long hair is a dishonor, but for a woman, long hair is her glory? Long hair was given to her to serve as a covering. If anyone wants to dispute it, we recognize no such custom, and neither do the churches of God.

The Lord’s Supper

But as I give you this next instruction, I do not praise you, because when you come together, it makes things worse, not better. To begin with, I am told that when you gather as a church you are split into groups, and I believe some of it. For factions among you are bound to come, so that those who stand the test may be seen for what they are. So when you gather in one place, what you eat is not really the Lord’s Supper. Each of you, as you eat, goes ahead with your own meal; one is left hungry, and another is drunk. Surely you have homes of your own for eating and drinking? Or do you look down on God’s church and shame those who have nothing? What am I to say to you? Should I praise you? In this matter, no, I do not praise you.

The bread and the cup

What I handed on to you, I myself received from the Lord: on the night he was handed over, the Lord Jesus took bread, gave thanks and broke it, saying, “This is my body; it is for you. Do this to remember me.” He did the same with the cup once supper was over, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Every time you drink it, do this to remember me.” For each time you eat this bread and drink the cup, you are announcing the Lord’s death, until he comes.

So whoever eats the bread or drinks the Lord’s cup in an unworthy way will be answerable for the Lord’s body and blood. Each of you should first examine yourself, and then eat of the bread and drink from the cup. Anyone who eats and drinks brings judgment on themselves by that eating and drinking, if they do not discern the body. This is the reason so many among you are weak and ill, and a good number have died. If we examined ourselves with discernment, we would not be coming under judgment. But when the Lord judges us, he is correcting us, to keep us from being condemned along with the world.

So, my brothers and sisters, when you meet for the meal, wait for each other. If someone is hungry, let them eat at home, so that your coming together does not lead to judgment.

The remaining matters I will set right when I come.

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 12
fields.body_html:
Gifts from the one Spirit

Now about spiritual gifts, brothers and sisters: I want you to be well informed. You know how it was when you were pagans: you were swept off to idols that cannot speak, carried away whichever way you were led. That is why I am making this clear to you: nobody who speaks through God’s Spirit ever says, “Jesus is cursed,” and nobody can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except through the Holy Spirit.

Gifts are given out in different ways, but it is the same Spirit who gives them. Ministries are given out in different ways, and it is the same Lord who is served. Workings of power are given out in different ways, but it is the same God who works all of them in everyone. Each person is given a way in which the Spirit is openly at work, and it is given for the good of all. Through the Spirit one person is given a message of wisdom; another, by the same Spirit, a message of knowledge; another, by the same Spirit, faith; another, by the one Spirit, gifts of healing; another, the power to work miracles; another, prophecy; another, the ability to tell spirits apart; another, different kinds of tongues; and another, the interpretation of tongues. One and the same Spirit is at work in all of these, giving to each person separately as he chooses.

One body with many parts

A body is a single whole, and yet it has many parts; all its parts, many as they are, make up one body. It is the same with Christ. Indeed, all of us were baptized in one Spirit into one body, whether we were Jews or Greeks, slaves or free, and all of us were given one Spirit to drink.

After all, a body does not consist of one part. It has many. Suppose the foot says, “I am not a hand, so I do not belong to the body.” Would it belong to the body any less for that? And if the ear says, “I am not an eye, so I do not belong to the body,” it does not belong to the body any less for that. If the body were nothing but an eye, how would it hear? If it were all ear, what would it smell with? But as things are, God has arranged each and every part in the body as he saw fit. If the whole were one single part, what kind of body would that be? As it is, the parts are many, but the body is one. So the eye cannot tell the hand, “I can do without you,” and the head cannot tell the feet, “I can do without you.” Quite the reverse. The parts of the body that seem weaker are all the more necessary. The parts we think deserve less honor are the very ones we clothe with greater honor, and the parts we do not show are covered with greater care for decency, while the parts we can show need no such care. But God has blended the body together and given more honor to the part that falls short, so that the body would not be split apart, but its parts would all care for one another alike. If one part is in pain, all the parts share its pain; if one part is honored, all the parts share its joy.

You are the body of Christ

You are Christ’s body, and each of you individually is one of its parts. In the church God has placed some people: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers. After them come miracles, then gifts of healing, the ability to help, the ability to guide, and different kinds of tongues. Is everyone an apostle? Is everyone a prophet? Is everyone a teacher? Does everyone work miracles? Does everyone have gifts of healing? Does everyone speak in tongues? Does everyone interpret? But set your hearts on the greater gifts. And now I will show you a way that is beyond comparison.

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 13
fields.body_html:
Without love, nothing

Suppose I speak in the tongues of human beings, and of angels too. If I do not have love, I am no more than booming bronze or a clashing cymbal. I may be able to prophesy, and know every mystery and everything there is to know; I may have all the faith there is, enough to move mountains; but if I do not have love, I am nothing. I may hand out everything I own as food for others; I may hand over my body to the flames; but if I do not have love, it does me no good at all.

Love is patient; love is kind. Love does not envy, does not show off, is not puffed up. It does not behave shamefully, it does not look for its own advantage, it does not lose its temper, and it does not keep a tally of wrongs. It takes no pleasure in wrongdoing, but shares the joy of the truth. There is nothing love cannot bear, no time when it stops believing or hoping, nothing it cannot endure.

Love never comes to an end

Love never comes to an end. But prophecies will be done away with; tongues will fall silent; knowledge will be done away with. For what we know is only partial, and our prophesying is partial too. But when what is complete arrives, what is partial will be done away with. When I was a child, I talked as a child talks, thought as a child thinks, and reasoned as a child reasons. But I am a man now, and I have done away with childish ways. For now we see by means of a mirror, as if in a riddle, but then we will see face to face. Now my knowledge is partial, but then I will know fully, as God has fully known me. As things are, then, three things last: faith, hope and love. And of these three, the greatest is love.

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 14
fields.body_html:
Prophecy builds up the church

Strive for love, and set your hearts on spiritual gifts, most of all on prophesying. Someone who speaks in a tongue is speaking not to people but to God. No one understands what is said; in the Spirit, the speaker is uttering mysteries. But someone who prophesies speaks to people, and the words build them up, encourage them and comfort them. Those who speak in a tongue build up themselves, but those who prophesy build up the church. I would be glad for all of you to speak in tongues, but gladder still for you to prophesy. Those who prophesy are greater than those who speak in tongues, unless they also interpret, so that the church receives something that builds it up.

So then, brothers and sisters, suppose I come to you speaking in tongues. What use will I be to you, unless what I say to you brings a revelation, or knowledge, or prophecy, or teaching? Think of instruments, lifeless as they are, that give out a sound, like the flute or the harp. If their notes are not distinct, how can anyone tell what is being played on the flute or the harp? And if a trumpet sounds a signal no one can make out, who will prepare to fight? So with you: if your tongue does not produce speech that makes sense, how will what you say be understood? You will be speaking to empty air. Who knows how many languages there are in the world? And not one of them is without meaning. If I do not understand the language someone speaks, we will be foreigners to each other: I to the speaker, and the speaker to me. It is the same with you. Since you are so eager for the workings of the Spirit, aim to have them in abundance for the building up of the church.

For that reason, anyone who speaks in a tongue should ask God for the power to interpret it as well. When I pray in a tongue, it is my spirit that prays, while my mind bears no fruit. What follows, then? I will pray in the spirit, and I will pray with my mind as well. I will sing praise in the spirit, and I will sing praise with my mind as well. Otherwise, if you bless God in the spirit, how will someone who is in the outsider’s place say the “Amen” to your prayer of thanks? That person has no idea what you are saying. Your thanksgiving may be fine, but it does nothing to build up the other person. I am thankful to God that, more than every one of you, I speak in tongues. But when the church meets, I would sooner speak five words with my mind, so as to teach others too, than thousands upon thousands of words in a tongue.

Tongues, prophecy and outsiders

Brothers and sisters, do not think like children. Be babies where evil is concerned, but in your understanding be grown up. It is written in the law: “Through those who speak other tongues, and through the lips of strangers, I will speak to this people; and not even then will they heed me, says the Lord.” So tongues serve as a sign, but the sign is for unbelievers, not for those who believe. Prophecy, on the other hand, is for those who believe, not for unbelievers. Picture the whole church gathered in one place, with everyone speaking in tongues. If outsiders or unbelievers walk in, will they not say you have gone mad? But if everyone is prophesying, and some unbeliever or outsider comes in, they are convicted by what all are saying and examined by what all are saying. The secrets of their heart come into the open, and so they will fall face down and worship God, declaring, “God really is among you!”

Order when the church meets

What follows, then, brothers and sisters? Whenever you gather, each of you has something: a psalm, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, an interpretation. Everything should be done to build up the church. As for speaking in a tongue, let it be done by two people, or by three at the most, each taking a turn, and let one person interpret. If there is no one to interpret, the speaker should keep silent in the church, speaking only to themselves and to God. As for prophets, let two or three speak, and let the others weigh their words. And if something is revealed to another person who is sitting there, the first speaker should keep silent. You can all prophesy, each in turn, so that all of you learn and all of you are encouraged. Prophets have their own spirits under their control. God is the God of peace, not of disorder, as is true in all the churches of God’s holy people.

In the churches the women are to keep silent. They are not permitted to speak; instead they are to be subject, as the law also says. If there is something they wish to learn, they are to put their questions to their own husbands at home. It is shameful for a woman to speak when the church meets. Or did God’s word go out from you? Has it come to you and no one else? If anyone thinks they are a prophet or spiritual, they should recognize that what I am writing to you comes from the Lord. Anyone who refuses to recognize this is not recognized either. So then, my brothers and sisters, set your hearts on prophesying, and do not stop anyone from speaking in tongues. But let everything be done properly and in good order.

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 15
fields.body_html:
The resurrection of Christ

Brothers and sisters, I am setting out for you once more the gospel I proclaimed to you. You received it, you stand firm in it, and through it you are being saved, if you keep hold of the message as I proclaimed it to you. Otherwise you came to believe for nothing.

What I handed on to you, as the first and chief thing, I myself had received: that Christ died for our sins, in keeping with the Scriptures; that he was buried; that he has been raised on the third day, in keeping with the Scriptures; and that he appeared to Cephas, and after that to the Twelve. Next he appeared to more than 500 brothers and sisters on a single occasion. Most of them are alive to this day, but some have died. Then he appeared to James, and after him to all the apostles. Last of all, as though to a child born before its time, he appeared to me as well. Among the apostles I am the least; I am not even fit to bear the name apostle, because I persecuted God’s church. It is God’s grace that has made me what I am, and his grace to me was not wasted. Instead, I have toiled harder than all of them, though it was not I but God’s grace working with me. In any case, whether it came from me or from them, this is the message we all proclaim, and this is the message you believed.

If the dead are not raised

Now if what we proclaim about Christ is that he has been raised from the dead, how can some among you be saying there is no such thing as a resurrection of the dead? If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised either. And if Christ has not been raised, then what we proclaim is empty, and your faith is empty too. Worse, we turn out to be giving false evidence about God, since we have borne witness against God by saying he raised Christ, when he did not raise him, if it is really so that the dead are not raised. For if dead people are not raised, neither has Christ been raised. But if Christ has not been raised, your faith is worthless, and you are still in your sins. It would also mean that those who have died in Christ have perished. If our hope in Christ reaches no further than this life, no one is more to be pitied than we are.

The firstfruits of those who have died

But as it is, Christ has been raised from the dead: he is the firstfruits of those who have died. For since death came by way of a human being, the resurrection of the dead also comes by way of a human being. Just as all who belong to Adam die, so all who belong to Christ will be brought to life. But each has a set place in the sequence: first Christ, the firstfruits; after that, at his coming, the people who are his. After that comes the end, when he hands the kingdom over to God the Father, once he has put an end to every ruler, every authority and every power. For his reign must continue until he has placed all his enemies beneath his feet. The last enemy to be done away with is death. For “he has placed everything in subjection beneath his feet.” Now when Scripture says that all things have been placed in subjection, it is obvious that this does not include the one who placed all things in subjection to him. And once all things have been made subject to him, the Son himself will then be made subject to the one who made all things subject to him, so that God may be all in all.

Otherwise, what will those who are baptized on behalf of the dead accomplish? If the dead are not raised at all, what is the point of being baptized for them? And why do we ourselves put our lives at risk hour after hour? I die every day. I swear it by how proud I am of you in Christ Jesus our Lord. If my fight with wild beasts in Ephesus was only for this life’s sake, what good has it done me? If the dead are not raised, then “Let us eat and drink, since tomorrow we die.” Make no mistake: “Good character is ruined by bad company.” Sober up, as you should, and stop sinning. There are some who do not know God at all. I say this to shame you.

The resurrection body

But someone will object, “How are dead people raised? And what sort of body will they have when they come back?” How foolish! A seed you sow does not come alive unless it dies. When you sow, you are not sowing the body that will grow, but a bare seed, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain. God gives it the body he has chosen, and gives each kind of seed a body of its own. Flesh is not all of one kind. Human flesh is one thing, the flesh of animals another, the flesh of birds another, and that of fish another. Some bodies belong to the heavens and some to the earth, and the glory of those in the heavens differs from the glory of those on earth. The sun has its own glory, the moon another, the stars another; and even among the stars, each has a glory that is different.

It is the same with the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in decay; it is raised imperishable. In dishonor it is sown, in glory it is raised; in weakness it is sown, in power it is raised. What is sown is a natural body; what is raised is a spiritual body.

If a natural body exists, a spiritual body exists too. This is also what Scripture says: “Adam, the first man, became a living being.” The last Adam became a spirit who gives life. The spiritual does not come first. The natural comes first, and the spiritual after it. The first man came from the earth and was made of dust; the second man comes from heaven. Everyone made of dust is like the man made of dust, and everyone who belongs to heaven is like the man from heaven. Just as we have worn the likeness of the man made of dust, so we will wear the likeness of the man from heaven.

Victory over death

What I mean, brothers and sisters, is this: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, and what decays cannot inherit what never decays. Listen, I am telling you a mystery. Not all of us will die, but all of us will be changed, in an instant, in the blink of an eye, when the last trumpet sounds. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised, never again to decay, and we who are alive will be changed. This perishable body has to put on imperishability like a garment, and this mortal body has to put on immortality. When this perishable body has put on imperishability and this mortal body has put on immortality, then the words written in Scripture will come true: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” Death, where is your victory? Death, where is your sting? Death’s sting is sin, and what gives sin its power is the law. But thanks be to God, for through our Lord Jesus Christ he gives us the victory.

So then, my dear brothers and sisters, be firm and unshakable, always doing more and more in the work of the Lord, since you know that in the Lord your hard work is never wasted.

fields.title: 1 Corinthians 16
fields.body_html:
The collection for God’s people

Now about the collection for God’s holy people: you are to follow the instructions I gave the churches in Galatia. On the first day of each week, every one of you should put something aside at home, saving as much as you have gained, so that there will be no need to take up collections when I arrive. When I arrive, I will send the people you have approved, with your letters to recommend them, to take your gift of grace to Jerusalem. If it seems right for me to go as well, they will travel with me.

Paul’s travel plans

I will come to you after I have gone through Macedonia, since my route lies through Macedonia. I may stay with you for a while, perhaps even for the winter. Then you can send me on, with what I need, to wherever I go next. This time I do not want to see you only briefly, on my way somewhere else; I hope to stay with you for a while, if the Lord allows. But I will stay on here in Ephesus until Pentecost. A great door stands open here for work that bears fruit, and many are working against me.

If Timothy comes, take care that he can be with you without fear, because the work he does is the Lord’s work, just as mine is. No one, then, should look down on him. See him off in peace, with what he needs for the road, so that he can come back to me; I am looking for him to return with the brothers.

As for our brother Apollos, I pressed him again and again to visit you along with the brothers. But he was not at all willing to come at this time; he will come when a good opportunity arises.

Final appeals and greetings

Stay alert. Hold your ground in the faith. Be brave and be strong. Whatever you do, do it in love.

I have a request, brothers and sisters. You know the household of Stephanas: they were the first of the harvest in Achaia, and they have set themselves to serve God’s holy people. I urge you in turn to place yourselves under people like these, and under everyone who joins in the work and labors hard. It makes me glad that Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus are here, because they have filled the gap your absence left. They have refreshed me in spirit, and you as well. Make sure, then, that people like these are honored.

Greetings to you from the churches of Asia. Warm greetings in the Lord from Aquila and Prisca and from the church that meets in their house. All the brothers and sisters here send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.

I, Paul, am adding this greeting with my own hand. A curse on anyone who does not love the Lord!

Our Lord, come! May the grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. I send my love to every one of you in Christ Jesus.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Stay alert. Hold your ground in the faith. Be brave and be strong. Whatever you do, do it in love.

— 1 Corinthians 16:13–14

After sixteen chapters of argument, rebuke and pleading, Paul sums up in a few short commands. Be steady; be brave; and do all of it in love. It is the letter in miniature. The Corinthians had plenty of courage, plenty of conviction and plenty of gifts. What they lacked was the love that would make all of it build up rather than tear down.

The question the letter leaves

The question 1 Corinthians leaves with its readers is not whether they are gifted, or knowledgeable, or free. The Corinthians were all three. It is what their gifts, knowledge and freedom are for. Again and again Paul answers: for others. Knowledge is for building up the brother or sister for whom Christ died. Freedom is for winning others. Gifts are for the good of all. Even Paul’s rights as an apostle are there to be given up “so as not to block the path of the gospel of Christ in any way.”

That is a hard word for any church that prizes its talent, its eloquence or its spiritual experiences, which is to say for most churches. It is also a freeing one. A church that is a body does not need every member to be an eye. It needs each part to care for the others, so that when one suffers, all suffer, and when one is honoured, all rejoice.

Where the letter points

It points back to the cross. Paul’s answer to a church dazzled by wisdom and status was not a better kind of wisdom but a crucified Messiah, who is “God’s power and God’s wisdom”. Every later section of the letter follows the same pattern of strength found in weakness: an apostle who works with his hands, a body whose weakest parts are most honoured, a love that does not look for its own advantage.

And it points forward to the resurrection. The Corinthians were tempted to think either that the body did not matter, or that the life of heaven was already theirs in full. Paul answers both with the risen Christ, the firstfruits of a harvest still to come. Because the body will be raised, what we do with it now matters. Because the end has not yet come, the church lives in hope, praying “Our Lord, come!” And because Christ has won, “in the Lord your hard work is never wasted.”

Where to go from here

Many of the church’s great preachers have returned to this letter, and a number of them are in this library. A few places to begin:

  • The church at Corinth, a generation later. The First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, written from the church in Rome around AD 96 to a congregation still divided, which tells them to take up Paul’s letter again.
  • On the wisdom of the cross (chapter 1). Charles H. Spurgeon’s Christ Crucified (1:23–24), George Whitefield’s Christ the Believer’s Wisdom, Righteousness, Sanctification and Redemption (1:30) and Jonathan Edwards’s God Glorified in Man’s Dependence (1:29–31).
  • On the race and the wilderness (chapters 9–10). Robert Murray M’Cheyne’s A Castaway (9:26–27) and Christmas Evans’s The Smitten Rock (10:4).
  • On the Spirit and his gifts (chapter 12). William J. Seymour’s Gifts of the Spirit (12:1), and in A. B. Simpson’s The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High, the New Testament volume, the chapters “The Holy Spirit in the First Epistle to the Corinthians” and “The Holy Spirit in the Body of Christ”.
  • On love (chapter 13). Henry Drummond’s The Greatest Thing in the World, Martin Luther’s Paul’s Praise of Christian Love and Corrie ten Boom’s The Greatest of These Is Love (13:13).
  • On the resurrection (chapter 15). Dwight L. Moody’s One Word—“Gospel” (15:1), John Newton’s The Lord Is Risen Indeed (15:20) and Frederick W. Robertson’s Victory over Death (15:56–57).

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to 1 Corinthians in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this letter.

And then read on, into 2 Corinthians, where the story continues: a painful visit, a letter written in tears, and a reconciliation that Paul could only call comfort. But first it may be worth reading chapter 13 once more, slowly, putting your own name where the word “love” stands, and seeing how far it still has to go. Paul would not mind. He ends, after all, with the three things that last:

As things are, then, three things last: faith, hope and love. And of these three, the greatest is love.

— 1 Corinthians 13:13
